rmt-2010-adv-01.title: Inclusion-exclusion
rmt-2010-adv-01.body:
Let $E$ be the event that the mathematician picks a duck egg: $P(E)=\frac25$. Let $H$ be the event that at least one of the two duck eggs hatches: $P(H)=1-\left(\frac23\right)^2=\frac59$. The events are independent, so
$$P(E\cup H)=\frac25+\frac59-\frac25\cdot\frac59=\frac25+\frac59-\frac29=\frac25+\frac13=\frac{11}{15}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{11}{15}$**

rmt-2010-adv-01.title: Complement
rmt-2010-adv-01.body:
She does not lose exactly when a non-duck egg is picked ($\frac35$) and neither duck egg hatches ($\frac23\cdot\frac23=\frac49$). That has probability $\frac35\cdot\frac49=\frac4{15}$, so she loses with probability $1-\frac4{15}=\frac{11}{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac{11}{15}$**

rmt-2010-adv-02.title: Geometric series
rmt-2010-adv-02.body:
The digits after the point have place values $(2i)^{-1},(2i)^{-2},\dots$. With $(2i)^{-1}=-\frac i2$, $(2i)^{-2}=-\frac14$, $(2i)^{-3}=\frac i8$, $(2i)^{-4}=\frac1{16}$, one block $0123$ is worth
$$0\cdot\left(-\tfrac i2\right)+1\cdot\left(-\tfrac14\right)+2\cdot\tfrac i8+3\cdot\tfrac1{16}=-\tfrac14+\tfrac i4+\tfrac3{16}=-\tfrac1{16}+\tfrac i4,$$
and the block repeats, each time multiplied by $(2i)^{-4}=\frac1{16}$. So the fractional part is $\frac{-\frac1{16}+\frac i4}{1-\frac1{16}}=\frac{16}{15}\left(-\frac1{16}+\frac i4\right)=-\frac1{15}+\frac{4i}{15}$.

Adding the integer part $3$: $\frac{44}{15}+\frac{4}{15}i$.

**Answer: $\frac{44}{15}+\frac4{15}i$**

rmt-2010-adv-02.title: Let the value be $v$
rmt-2010-adv-02.body:
Let $v=0.\overline{0123}_{2i}$. Moving the point four places to the right multiplies by $(2i)^4=16$ and gives $16v=0123_{2i}+v$, where $0123_{2i}=1\cdot(2i)^2+2\cdot(2i)+3=-4+4i+3=-1+4i$. So $15v=-1+4i$, $v=-\frac1{15}+\frac{4i}{15}$, and the number is $3+v=\frac{44}{15}+\frac4{15}i$.

**Answer: $\frac{44}{15}+\frac4{15}i$**

rmt-2010-adv-03.title: Six people suffice
rmt-2010-adv-03.body:
Take any person $P$ among $6$. Of the other $5$ people, either at least $3$ met $P$ last year or at least $3$ did not (pigeonhole). Suppose $A,B,C$ all met $P$ (the other case is symmetric). If two of $A,B,C$ met each other, those two and $P$ all met each other. Otherwise $A,B,C$ did not meet each other. Either way we get the required three people.

Five people are not enough: arrange them in a pentagon and say two met iff they are adjacent. Any three people include two non-adjacent and two adjacent ones, so no three mutually met and no three mutually unmet.

**Answer: 6**

rmt-2010-adv-03.title: Graph language
rmt-2010-adv-03.body:
This is the Ramsey number $R(3,3)=6$: every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_6$ contains a monochromatic triangle, while the colouring of $K_5$ with the pentagon in red and the pentagram in blue has none.

**Answer: 6**

rmt-2010-adv-04.title: Multiple-angle identities
rmt-2010-adv-04.body:
Use $\cos^3\theta=\frac{3\cos\theta+\cos3\theta}4$ and the product formula $\cos^2\theta=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}2$: $\cos^5\theta=\cos^3\theta\cdot\cos^2\theta=\frac{3\cos\theta+\cos3\theta}{4}\cdot\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}$. Expanding with $\cos a\cos b=\frac{\cos(a+b)+\cos(a-b)}2$ gives $\frac18\left[3\cos\theta+\cos3\theta+\frac32(\cos3\theta+\cos\theta)+\frac12(\cos5\theta+\cos\theta)\right]=\frac18\left[5\cos\theta+\frac52\cos3\theta+\frac12\cos5\theta\right]$, the same result.

**Answer: $\frac1{16}\cos5\theta+\frac5{16}\cos3\theta+\frac58\cos\theta$**

rmt-2010-adv-05.title: Hockey stick
rmt-2010-adv-05.body:
By the hockey stick identity $\sum_{i=j}^{2010}\binom ij=\binom{2011}{j+1}$. So the sum is $\sum_{j=0}^{2010}\binom{2011}{j+1}=\sum_{m=1}^{2011}\binom{2011}m=2^{2011}-1$.

**Answer: $2^{2011}-1$**

rmt-2010-adv-05.title: Counting subsets
rmt-2010-adv-05.body:
$\sum_{i=0}^{2010}\sum_{j=0}^{i}\binom ij=\sum_{i=0}^{2010}2^i=2^{2011}-1$, by summing over $i$ first (the inner sum is the number of subsets of an $i$-element set) and then the geometric series.

**Answer: $2^{2011}-1$**

rmt-2010-adv-06.title: Factor the equation
rmt-2010-adv-06.body:
The number of blue cells is $n+m-1$ out of $nm$, so $2010(n+m-1)=nm$, i.e. $nm-2010n-2010m+2010=0$, which is
$$(n-2010)(m-2010)=2010\cdot2009.$$
Both factors cannot be negative: then $|n-2010|\le2009$ and $|m-2010|\le2009$ (as $n,m\ge1$), so the product would be at most $2009^2<2010\cdot2009$. They cannot have opposite signs since the product is positive. So both factors are positive divisors of $2010\cdot2009=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot67\cdot7^2\cdot41$, and each divisor $n-2010$ gives exactly one pair $(n,m)$. The number of divisors is $2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot2=96$.

**Answer: 96**

rmt-2010-adv-07.title: Branching process
rmt-2010-adv-07.body:
Let $q$ be the probability of dying out. The bug dies (probability $1-p$) or splits (probability $p$) and both copies' lines die out (probability $q^2$ by independence): $q=(1-p)+pq^2$, i.e. $pq^2-q+(1-p)=0$, with roots $q=1$ and $q=\frac{1-p}p$.

Which root? Let $q_n$ be the probability of dying out within $n$ generations: $q_0=0$ and $q_{n+1}=(1-p)+pq_n^2$. The true $q$ is $\lim q_n$. Put $r=\frac{1-p}p<1$ (since $p>\frac12$). Then $q_0<r$, and if $q_k<r$ then $q_{k+1}=(1-p)+pq_k^2<(1-p)+pr^2=r$ (because $r$ is a root). So $q_n<r$ for all $n$, and $q=\lim q_n\le r<1$. Hence $q=r=\frac{1-p}p$.

**Answer: $\frac{1-p}p$**

rmt-2010-adv-07.title: Check with an example
rmt-2010-adv-07.body:
For $p=\frac23$ the formula gives $\frac{1/3}{2/3}=\frac12$. Iterating $q_{n+1}=\frac13+\frac23q_n^2$ from $0$ gives $0,\ 0.333,\ 0.408,\ 0.442,\ 0.464,\dots\to0.5$, consistent with $\frac{1-p}p$ (and not with $1$).

**Answer: $\frac{1-p}p$**

rmt-2010-adv-08.title: Finite differences
rmt-2010-adv-08.body:
For a polynomial of degree $n$, the $(n+1)$-th finite difference vanishes: $\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}(-1)^{n+1-k}\binom{n+1}kP(k)=0$. Hence
$$P(n+1)=-\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^{n+1-k}\binom{n+1}kP(k)=-\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^{n+1-k}\binom{n+1}k3^k.$$
By the binomial theorem $\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}(-1)^{n+1-k}\binom{n+1}k3^k=(3-1)^{n+1}=2^{n+1}$, so the sum up to $n$ is $2^{n+1}-3^{n+1}$ and $P(n+1)=3^{n+1}-2^{n+1}$.

**Answer: $3^{n+1}-2^{n+1}$**

rmt-2010-adv-10.title: Cases mod 5
rmt-2010-adv-10.body:
Since $\lfloor n^2/5\rfloor$ is even in $n$, it suffices to find the $n\ge0$ that work. Write $n=5a+r$ with $r\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}$, so $\lfloor n^2/5\rfloor=5a^2+2ar+\lfloor r^2/5\rfloor$:

- $r=0$: $5a^2$, prime only for $a=1$ ($n=5$, value $5$).
- $r=1$: $a(5a+2)$, prime only for $a=1$ ($n=6$, value $7$).
- $r=2$: $a(5a+4)$, prime only for $a=1$, but $9$ is not prime ($n=7$).
- $r=3$: $(5a+1)(a+1)$, never prime ($a=0$ gives $1$; $a\ge1$ gives two factors $\ge2$).
- $r=4$: $(5a+3)(a+1)$, prime only for $a=0$ ($n=4$, value $3$).

So the $n\ge0$ are $4,5,6$ and the integers are $\pm4,\pm5,\pm6$, with product $(-16)(-25)(-36)=-14400$.

**Answer: $-14400$**

rmt-2010-adv-10.title: Check by listing
rmt-2010-adv-10.body:
Listing $\lfloor n^2/5\rfloor$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots,9$ gives $0,0,0,1,3,5,7,9,12,16$, so the primes occur at $n=4,5,6$ (values $3,5,7$); the factorisation above shows no larger $n$ works. By symmetry $-4,-5,-6$ also work, and the product is $4\cdot5\cdot6\cdot(-4)(-5)(-6)=-14400$.

**Answer: $-14400$**
